disclaimer: This information is educational and general. A model prediction is not a confirmed diagnosis. Local conditions, crop variety and regulations matter, so confirm with a local agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist before treating crops.

bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
bacterial_spot.summary: Caused by Xanthomonas bacteria. It spreads in warm, wet weather through splashing water, infected seed and transplants, and contaminated tools or hands.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that may turn brown or black
Spots can have a yellow halo and may tear out, leaving a shot-hole look
Raised, scabby spots on green fruit
prevention: Start with certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base
Do not handle plants while foliage is wet
Rotate away from tomato and pepper for at least 2 to 3 years
Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest
care: Space and stake plants so leaves dry quickly
Remove heavily affected leaves and dispose of them away from the garden
Disinfect tools between plants
bacterial_spot.expert_advice: If spots keep spreading, reach fruit, or you grow tomatoes commercially, ask a local extension service which control options are approved and effective in your area.

early_blight.name: Early blight
early_blight.summary: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It usually starts on older, lower leaves and is favoured by warm weather with alternating wet and dry periods.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings, like a target
Yellowing of tissue around the spots; lower leaves die first
Dark, sunken lesions on stems or near the fruit stalk
prevention: Rotate crops and avoid planting tomatoes or potatoes in the same spot every year
Mulch to reduce soil splash
Use drip or base watering
Remove lower leaves touching the soil and clear plant debris
Keep plants well nourished and not water-stressed
care: Prune lower leaves and stake plants for airflow
Remove infected leaves early
Avoid working among wet plants
early_blight.expert_advice: If more than a few lower leaves are affected, or the disease reaches upper leaves, stems or fruit, consult a local expert about management suited to your region.

late_blight.name: Late blight
late_blight.summary: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. It spreads very fast in cool, humid or rainy weather and can destroy plants within days. It also affects potatoes.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked patches that turn dark brown or greenish-grey
White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Firm, brown, greasy-looking patches on fruit
Dark lesions on stems
prevention: Use healthy transplants and resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead watering and improve airflow
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants
Check plants often during cool, wet spells
care: Remove and bag suspected plants promptly; do not compost them
Do not move infected plant material between plots
late_blight.expert_advice: Treat suspected late blight as urgent. Contact a local extension service or plant clinic quickly, because it can spread to neighbouring tomato and potato crops.

leaf_mold.name: Leaf mold
leaf_mold.summary: Caused by the fungus Passalora fulva. It thrives in high humidity and poor airflow, and is especially common in greenhouses and tunnels.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brownish velvety mold on the underside of the same spots
Leaves curl, wither and drop in severe cases
prevention: Ventilate greenhouses and tunnels to reduce humidity
Space plants and prune for airflow
Water at the base, early in the day
Choose resistant varieties where available
Clean up plant debris at season end
care: Remove affected leaves
Avoid wetting foliage
leaf_mold.expert_advice: If it keeps returning in a greenhouse or spreads to many plants, ask an expert about humidity management and suitable varieties for your setup.

mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus
mosaic_virus.summary: A very stable virus that spreads mainly by hands, tools, plant contact and contaminated seed or debris. There is no cure for infected plants.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green patches on leaves
Distorted, narrow or fern-like leaves
Stunted growth and uneven fruit ripening
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties where available
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools between plants
Avoid handling tobacco products before touching plants
Remove infected plants and weeds nearby
Do not reuse stakes or trays without cleaning them
care: Handle healthy plants before suspected ones
Bag and discard infected plants; do not compost
mosaic_virus.expert_advice: Virus symptoms can resemble herbicide drift or nutrient problems. Ask an expert to confirm, because the right response depends on the exact cause.

septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It usually appears on lower leaves after fruit set and spreads by splashing water in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Many small, round spots with dark borders and grey-white centers
Tiny black specks inside the spot centers
Lower leaves yellow, wither and fall, exposing fruit to sunburn
prevention: Rotate crops and avoid planting tomatoes in the same place each year
Mulch and water at the base
Remove lower leaves and plant debris
Space and stake plants for airflow
care: Remove affected leaves early
Avoid handling wet plants
septoria_leaf_spot.expert_advice: If defoliation is spreading upward or affecting yield, ask a local expert about control options suited to your region.

spider_mites.name: Spider mites (two-spotted)
spider_mites.summary: Tiny sap-feeding mites that build up in hot, dry, dusty conditions. They are a pest, so the damage is caused by feeding rather than by an infection.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves
Bronzed, dry-looking leaves that may curl and drop
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves or between stems in heavy infestations
prevention: Check leaf undersides regularly with a hand lens
Avoid drought stress; keep plants evenly watered
Reduce dust around plants
Protect natural enemies such as predatory mites and ladybirds
care: On small plantings, a firm spray of water on the leaf undersides can reduce numbers
Remove heavily infested leaves
spider_mites.expert_advice: Mite problems can escalate quickly in hot weather. Ask a local expert about control options that are safe for beneficial insects and suitable for your region.

target_spot.name: Target spot
target_spot.summary: Caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It favours warm, humid weather and can affect leaves, stems and fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings and sometimes a yellow halo
Spots that merge and cause leaves to die
Sunken, pitted spots on fruit
prevention: Rotate crops and clear plant debris
Water at the base and avoid wetting leaves
Prune and space plants for airflow
Control weeds that hold moisture
care: Remove affected lower leaves
Do not work in the crop when leaves are wet
target_spot.expert_advice: Target spot looks very similar to early blight. Ask a local expert to confirm the cause before choosing a management plan.

yellow_leaf_curl_virus.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
yellow_leaf_curl_virus.summary: Spread by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Infected plants cannot be cured, and early infection can greatly reduce yield.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and become small and crinkled
Yellowing along leaf edges
Stunted, bushy plants and flower drop
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Use fine insect-proof netting over seedlings and young plants
Monitor whiteflies, for example with yellow sticky traps
Remove infected plants and nearby weeds that host whiteflies
Do not move plants from infested areas
care: Remove and bag infected plants early to reduce spread
Inspect new transplants before planting
yellow_leaf_curl_virus.expert_advice: If this virus is suspected, contact a local extension service. Whitefly control and resistant varieties are most effective when coordinated across a whole area.

healthy.name: Healthy leaf
healthy.category: No disease detected by the model
healthy.summary: The model did not find signs of the conditions it knows. This does not rule out other problems, such as very early infection, nutrient deficiency, or diseases the model was not trained on.
symptoms: Even green color, no spots, curling or distortion
prevention: Water at the base and avoid wetting leaves
Keep good airflow with spacing and pruning
Rotate crops and remove plant debris
Inspect plants weekly, including leaf undersides
care: Feed and water consistently
Re-check the plant if you notice any new spots or changes
healthy.expert_advice: If the plant still looks unwell, ask a local expert or take clearer photos from several leaves.
